closing.title: Why the cut after 33
closing.html:
The six ⭐ plurals are scattered across the whole episode (20, 23, 25, 38, 40, 43), so any positional cut splits the grammar point. Cutting after 33 splits it evenly — glazen, goederen, chemici in part 1; steden, medici, data in part 2 — so both days drill the same rule on fresh material instead of one day getting all of it. The focus candidates also split roughly evenly, and it lands on a scene boundary: part 1 is the job-interview conversation, part 2 is the scheduling conversation with Natasha.

  • Part 1 — sentences 1–33, run 2c with --max_unknown_words 15 (cum at s33 is 16). 10 real new words after dropping boilerplate and names.
  • Part 2 — sentences 34–57, second 2c run on the same LESSON_NUMBER with a bigger budget. ~12 real new words. Publish with KIND=pimsleur PART=2, never KIND=both.

Three parts is possible (cut after 25 and 43) but part 3 would carry only 5 words. Too thin.

sentences.nl: Welkom bij aflevering 4 van het tweede seizoen van Heb je Zin.
sentences.en: Welcome to episode 4 of the second season of Are You in the Mood.
sentences.note: Boilerplate.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Welcome to episode 4 of the second season of Have you Zin.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Welkom bij" means "welcome to" and is a standard greeting formula.  
• "Aflevering" means "episode," often used in the context of TV or radio shows.  
• "Van" is a preposition meaning "of," indicating possession or relation.  
• "Het tweede seizoen" means "the second season," where "het" is the definite article for neuter nouns, "tweede" is the ordinal number "second," and "seizoen" means "season."  
• "Heb je Zin" is a title, but "heb je zin" can also mean "are you in the mood" or "do you feel like it" in a more general context.

### Examples  
• Welkom bij de opening van het nieuwe museum. (Welcome to the opening of the new museum.)  
• Hij is de regisseur van de populaire serie. (He is the director of the popular series.)  
• Heb je zin in een kopje koffie? (Do you feel like a cup of coffee?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Welkom bij de presentatie van ons nieuwste product. (Welcome to the presentation of our newest product.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Dutch TV shows and series often have multiple seasons, and it's common for audiences to follow them closely, similar to other Western cultures. The phrase "Heb je Zin" also plays on a common Dutch expression, which can make it a catchy and relatable title.

sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we de grammatica van #dutchgrammar 1 les 44 en 45 over speciale vormen van het meervoud.
sentences.en: Today we are practicing the grammar from #dutchgrammar lesson 44 and 45 about special forms of the plural.
sentences.note: Boilerplate — but read it once: it names the grammar point (Gr.1 les 44+45).
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Today practice we the grammar of #dutchgrammar 1 lesson 44 and 45 about special forms of the plural.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence starts with "Vandaag" for emphasis on time, leading to inversion where the verb "oefenen" comes before the subject "we".  
• "Grammatica van #dutchgrammar 1 les 44 en 45" specifies the subject being practiced, showing a typical Dutch possessive structure with "van".  
• "Speciale vormen van het meervoud" highlights the topic, using "van" again to indicate the type of forms.

Extra examples:  
• Morgen gaan we naar de markt. (Tomorrow we go to the market.)  
• We lezen het boek van de bibliotheek. (We read the book from the library.)  
• Hij spreekt over de verschillende soorten kaas. (He talks about the different types of cheese.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Vandaag bezoeken we het museum van moderne kunst. (Today we visit the museum of modern art.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• #dutchgrammar is a popular online resource for learning Dutch, providing lessons and exercises.

sentences.nl: Xing loopt naar haar huisje.
sentences.en: Xing walks to her little house.
sentences.note: Simple SVO warm-up.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing walks to her little house.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Loopt" is the third-person singular present tense of "lopen" (to walk).  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "to" or "towards."  
• "Huisje" is a diminutive form of "huis" (house), often used to convey endearment or small size. In Dutch, adding "-je" or "-tje" is common to create diminutives.  
• Examples:  
  - Hij loopt naar de winkel. (He walks to the store.)  
  - Zij loopt naar haar vriend. (She walks to her friend.)  
  - Zij woont in een klein huisje. (She lives in a small house.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De kat loopt naar zijn mandje. (The cat walks to its little basket.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of diminutives like "huisje" is quite common in Dutch to express affection or to describe something as small or cute.

sentences.nl: Ze gaat haar koffer pakken.
sentences.en: She is going to pack her suitcase.
sentences.note: Already in your collocation library (met, 2026-07-30). gaan + inf = near future.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• She goes her suitcase pack.  

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ze gaat" is in the present tense and uses the verb "gaan" (to go) to indicate a future action, similar to "going to" in English.  
• "Haar koffer" translates to "her suitcase," showing possession with "haar" (her).  
• The verb "pakken" means "to pack" and is in the infinitive form because it's part of the future construction with "gaat."  
• Example: "Ik ga mijn tas inpakken." (I am going to pack my bag.)  
• Example: "Wij gaan morgen naar Amsterdam." (We are going to Amsterdam tomorrow.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Hij gaat zijn fiets repareren. (He is going to repair his bike.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Packing a suitcase is a common activity associated with travel, which is a popular pastime in the Netherlands due to its central location in Europe. Many Dutch people travel frequently for leisure or business.

haar.form_note: possessive pronoun for third person singular feminine

sentences.nl: Annika woont in hetzelfde huisje als Xing.
sentences.en: Annika lives in the same house as Xing.
sentences.note: hetzelfde X als Y — comparison frame.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Annika lives in the same house as Xing.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Woont" is the third person singular present tense of "wonen" (to live).  
• "In hetzelfde huisje" uses "hetzelfde" as a demonstrative pronoun meaning "the same," and "huisje" is the diminutive form of "huis" (house), implying a smaller or more cozy house.  
• "Als" is used here as a comparative conjunction meaning "as" or "like."

• Example: "Hij heeft hetzelfde boek als ik." (He has the same book as I do.)  
• Example: "We wonen in een groot huis." (We live in a big house.)  
• Example: "Zij werkt in hetzelfde kantoor als haar broer." (She works in the same office as her brother.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Jeroen eet hetzelfde broodje als zijn vriendin. (Jeroen eats the same sandwich as his girlfriend.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, living in a "huisje," which is often a cozy small house or cottage, can be quite common in rural areas or among those who prefer a quaint lifestyle.

sentences.nl: En Marieke is bij haar op bezoek.
sentences.en: And Marieke is visiting her.
sentences.note: bij haar op bezoek — note the word order: prep phrase splits the chunk.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And Marieke is at her on visit.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "En" (and) is a coordinating conjunction used to connect clauses or sentences.  
• "Bij haar op bezoek" is a phrase meaning "visiting her," where "bij" (at) denotes location, "haar" (her) is the object pronoun, and "op bezoek" (on visit) is a fixed expression for visiting someone.  
• Word Order: The sentence follows the Subject-Verb-Object order typical in Dutch main clauses.

Examples:  
• Ik ben bij hem op bezoek. (I am visiting him.)  
• Zij gaat bij haar oma op bezoek. (She is visiting her grandmother.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• En Pieter is bij zijn vriend op bezoek. (And Pieter is visiting his friend.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it's common to visit friends and family regularly, often announced in advance, but spontaneous visits are also quite accepted.

bezoek.form_note: no plural form in this context

sentences.nl: De dames hebben al best veel drank op.
sentences.en: The ladies have already had quite a lot to drink.
sentences.note: Separable op hebben = to have drunk. Particle lands at the very end.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• The ladies have already quite a lot of drink finished.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hebben...op" is a separable verb construction where "op" (meaning "up" or "finished") is placed at the end of the sentence.  
• "Best veel" is an informal way to express "quite a lot."  
• "Al" means "already," indicating something that has happened sooner than expected.

Examples:  
• "Hij heeft de taart al op." (He has already finished the cake.)  
• "Ze heeft best veel boeken gelezen." (She has read quite a lot of books.)  
• "Wij hebben al gegeten." (We have already eaten.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De heren hebben al best veel werk gedaan. (The gentlemen have already done quite a lot of work.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, drinking, especially social drinking, is common in social settings, but it is often done responsibly. The phrase might be used humorously to describe a lively social gathering.

de.form_note: definite article for common gender nouns

grammarHits.explanation: Drank (drink) is uncountable: 'veel drank', never 'veel dranken'. Same pattern as the slide's 'veel koffie'.

sentences.nl: De wodka van Annika smaakt goed.
sentences.en: Annika's vodka tastes good.
sentences.note: smaakt goed, not smaakt goed uit. Adjective bare after smaken.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• The vodka of Annika tastes good.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "De wodka van Annika" uses a possessive structure with "van" to indicate ownership ("the vodka of Annika").  
• "Smaakt" is the third person singular present tense of "smaken" (to taste).  
• The sentence follows the Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) order typical of Dutch main clauses.

• Extra examples:  
  - "De auto van Pieter is snel." (The car of Pieter is fast.)  
  - "Het huis van mijn ouders is groot." (The house of my parents is big.)  
  - "De koffie van dit café is sterk." (The coffee of this cafe is strong.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• De wijn van Marieke ruikt heerlijk. (The wine of Marieke smells delightful.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Vodka is not traditionally a Dutch drink; the Netherlands is more known for genever, a juniper-flavored spirit, which is considered a precursor to gin.

de.form_note: definite article for common gender singular nouns

wodka.form_note: singular noun; no special plural form

grammarHits.explanation: Wodka is an uncountable substance, so the verb is singular: smaakt. Mirrors the slide sentence 'De koffie smaakt goed'.

sentences.nl: Xing komt binnen.
sentences.en: Xing comes in.
sentences.note: Separable — komt … binnen, particle to the end.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing comes in.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Komt" is the third person singular present tense of "komen" (to come).  
• "Binnen" is an adverb meaning "inside" or "in," showing direction towards the interior of a place.  
• Dutch word order often places the verb in the second position in simple declarative sentences.

Extra Examples:  
• "Hij komt binnen." (He comes in.)  
• "Zij gaat naar binnen." (She goes inside.)  
• "De hond rent naar buiten." (The dog runs outside.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Anna komt ook binnen." (Anna also comes in.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)

sentences.nl: Wat leuk dat je op bezoek bent.
sentences.en: How nice that you are visiting.
sentences.note: Wat leuk dat + clause — verb goes to the END of the dat-clause.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• What nice that you on visit are.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wat leuk" is an expression meaning "How nice" or "That's nice." "Wat" is used here to express an exclamation.  
• "Dat" functions as a conjunction meaning "that," connecting two clauses.  
• "Op bezoek zijn" is a common expression meaning "to be on a visit" or "to visit." The preposition "op" is used with "bezoek" (visit).  
• Example 1: "Wat fijn dat je er bent." (How nice that you are here.)  
• Example 2: "Hij is op bezoek bij zijn oma." (He is visiting his grandmother.)  

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wat jammer dat je niet kon komen." (What a pity that you couldn't come.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, visiting friends and family is a common and valued social activity, often involving coffee and cake. It's polite to express enthusiasm when someone visits.

bezoek.form_note: noun used as part of a fixed expression

sentences.nl: Xing, waar was je? — We hebben jou de hele avond niet gezien.
sentences.en: Xing, where were you? — We haven't seen you all evening.
sentences.note: Perfect tense with hebben + past participle at the end.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing, where were you? — We have you the whole evening not seen.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Waar was je?" uses the simple past tense "was" (were) to ask about a past location or state.  
• "We hebben...niet gezien" is present perfect tense, with "hebben" (have) as the auxiliary verb and "gezien" (seen) as the past participle. This tense is used for actions completed in the past with relevance to the present.  
• "De hele avond" means "the whole evening," where "de" is the definite article, and "hele" is an adjective meaning "whole" or "entire."  
• Examples:  
  - "Waar was je gisteren?" (Where were you yesterday?)  
  - "Ik heb de film niet gezien." (I have not seen the movie.)  
  - "We hebben de hele dag gewacht." (We have waited the whole day.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Waar was je vanmiddag? — We hebben je bij de lunch niet gezien." (Where were you this afternoon? — We did not see you at lunch.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it's common to address someone directly by their name in conversation for clarity and politeness, especially in informal contexts.

sentences.nl: Heb je Martin misschien gezien? — Eh hm.
sentences.en: Have you seen Martin by any chance? — Uh hm.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Have you Martin maybe seen? — Uh huh.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• This sentence uses a question structure starting with the verb "Heb" (Have), which is typical for forming yes/no questions in Dutch.  
• The word "misschien" means "maybe" and is used to soften the question, making it less direct.  
• "Eh hm" is an informal way to acknowledge or agree, similar to "uh huh" in English.

Examples:  
• Heb je dat boek gelezen? (Have you read that book?)  
• Hebben jullie misschien tijd voor koffie? (Do you perhaps have time for coffee?)  
• Heeft zij de opdracht al af? (Has she finished the assignment yet?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Heb je de film misschien al gezien? (Have you maybe already seen the movie?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch conversation, using "misschien" in questions is common to make requests or questions less direct and more polite.

sentences.nl: Xing heeft Martin beloofd om niets over hun romantische avond te zeggen.
sentences.en: Xing promised Martin not to say anything about their romantic evening.
sentences.note: om … te + infinitive, verb final. Also niets … over split across the clause.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Xing has Martin promised to nothing about their romantic evening to say.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "heeft...beloofd" is the present perfect tense of "beloven" (to promise). Dutch often uses the auxiliary verb "hebben" or "zijn" with a past participle to form this tense.  
• "om...te zeggen" is an infinitive construction where "om" introduces the infinitive "te zeggen" (to say). This structure is often used to express purpose or intention.  
• "niets over" (nothing about) shows a negation with "niets" (nothing) and the preposition "over" (about).

- Zij heeft hem gevraagd om morgen te komen. (She has asked him to come tomorrow.)
- De leraar heeft de studenten beloofd om de toets uit te stellen. (The teacher has promised the students to postpone the test.)
- Hij heeft niets over de plannen gezegd. (He has said nothing about the plans.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Maria heeft Jan gevraagd om het geheim te bewaren. (Maria has asked Jan to keep the secret.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, directness is valued, and promises are generally taken seriously. If someone promises not to speak about something, it is typically expected that they will keep that promise.

romantische.form_note: inflected form for de-words or plural nouns

sentences.nl: Dus zegt ze: "Eh nee, ik heb Martin niet gezien.
sentences.en: So she says: "Uh no, I haven't seen Martin."
sentences.note: Dus fronted → inversion (zegt ze). You dropped this pattern on 07-30.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Thus says she: "Uh no, I have Martin not seen."

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence starts with "Dus" (Thus), which is often used to draw a conclusion or continuation from a previous statement.  
• The construction "zegt ze" (says she) uses inverted word order, which is common in reported speech.  
• "Eh nee" (Uh no) is an informal way of expressing hesitation or thinking before disagreeing.  
• The phrase "ik heb Martin niet gezien" (I have Martin not seen) uses the present perfect tense, which is formed by combining "heb" (have) with the past participle "gezien" (seen).  
• Example: "Dus zegt hij: 'Ik ben het vergeten.'" (Thus says he: "I have forgotten it.")  
• Example: "Eh ja, ik denk van wel." (Uh yes, I think so.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dus zegt hij: "Eh ja, ik kom morgen." (Thus says he: "Uh yes, I will come tomorrow.")

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch conversations, using fillers like "eh" or "uh" is common and signals that the speaker is thinking. This is similar to the use of "um" or "uh" in English.

sentences.nl: Wil je ook een glaasje wodka? — Op het aanrecht staan nog glazen.
sentences.en: Would you like a glass of vodka as well? — There are still glasses on the countertop.
sentences.note: ⭐ glas → glazen. Also: Op het aanrecht staan nog glazen — fronted place → inversion, and Dutch uses staan, not zijn, for upright objects.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Wil je ook een glaasje wodka? — Op het aanrecht staan nog glazen.  
  (Want you also a small glass vodka? — On the counter stand still glasses.)

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wil je" is an informal way to ask if someone wants something, using the verb "willen" (to want).  
• "Glaasje" is a diminutive form of "glas," indicating a small or endearing glass. Diminutives are common in Dutch to indicate size or affection.  
• "Op het aanrecht" specifies a location using the preposition "op" (on) and the definite article "het" (the) for a neuter noun.  
• "Staan nog glazen" uses inverted word order because the sentence starts with a prepositional phrase, and "nog" indicates "still" or "more."  
• Examples:  
  - "Heb je nog een kopje koffie?" (Do you want another cup of coffee?)  
  - "Op de tafel ligt een boek." (On the table lies a book.)  
  - "Er staan nog veel mensen buiten." (There are still many people outside.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wil je nog een stukje taart? — In de keuken staan meer borden."  
  (Do you want another piece of cake? — In the kitchen, there are more plates.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Offering drinks like "wodka" during social gatherings is common in Dutch culture, especially during toasts or special occasions. The use of diminutives like "glaasje" can make the offer sound more casual or friendly.

wil.form_note: conjugated in present tense, 2nd person singular

staan.form_note: conjugated in present tense, 3rd person plural

glazen.form_note: plural of glas: s becomes z, add -en

grammarHits.explanation: Plural of het glas. The short a becomes long in the open syllable gla-, and s becomes z.

sentences.nl: Nou nee, dankje.
sentences.en: Well no, thank you.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Now no, thanks.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Nou" is an informal interjection often used to start a sentence, similar to "well" in English.  
• "Nee" is a straightforward negation meaning "no."  
• "Dankje" is the informal way to say "thank you," where "je" is the informal diminutive suffix.  
• Example phrases:  
  - "Nou, ik moet gaan." (Well, I have to go.)  
  - "Nee, ik heb geen tijd." (No, I don’t have time.)  
  - "Dankje voor je hulp." (Thank you for your help.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Nou, ik weet het niet. (Well, I don't know.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, "dankje" is used in informal settings among friends and family. "Dank u" or "dankuwel" would be more appropriate in formal contexts.

sentences.nl: Ik moet mijn koffer nog pakken en volgende week is een belangrijke week voor mij.
sentences.en: I still need to pack my suitcase and next week is an important week for me.
sentences.note: Verb-final under a modal (moet … pakken) — you dropped this TWICE on 07-30. Then en volgende week is = fronted time → inversion.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I must my suitcase still pack and next week is an important week for me.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik moet" is a modal verb construction meaning "I must" or "I have to," followed by an infinitive verb.  
• "Mijn koffer" means "my suitcase," where "mijn" indicates possession.  
• "Nog pakken" means "still pack," where "nog" indicates something yet to be done.  
• "Volgende week" means "next week," a time expression often found at the start or end of a sentence.  
• "Is een belangrijke week voor mij" uses the adjective "belangrijke" (important) to describe "week," followed by "voor mij" (for me) to indicate personal relevance.  

Extra examples:  
• "Ik moet nog naar de winkel gaan." (I still have to go to the store.)  
• "Volgende maand hebben we een vakantie gepland." (Next month we have a holiday planned.)  
• "Dit is een belangrijk moment voor ons." (This is an important moment for us.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ik moet mijn paspoort niet vergeten en morgen is een lange dag voor mij." (I must not forget my passport and tomorrow is a long day for me.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• No culture note applicable.

sentences.nl: Oh, wat ga je doen? — Ik heb een sollicitatiegesprek bij een bedrijf dat goederen uit China importeert.
sentences.en: Oh, what are you going to do? — I have a job interview at a company that imports goods from China.
sentences.note: ⭐ goed → goederen (goods, ≠ good). Relative dat … importeert, verb final.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Oh, what go you do? — I have a job interview at a company that goods from China imports.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wat ga je doen?" uses the structure of "wat" (what) followed by the verb "gaan" (to go) and subject "je" (you), which is a common way to ask about future plans.  
• "Ik heb een sollicitatiegesprek" includes "hebben" (to have) in the present tense, which is used to indicate possession or current state.  
• "Bij een bedrijf dat goederen uit China importeert" uses a relative clause with "dat" (that) to give more information about the company. The verb "importeren" is in the present tense to describe a habitual action.

• Wat ga je morgen doen? (What are you going to do tomorrow?)  
• Ik heb een afspraak bij de dokter. (I have an appointment at the doctor.)  
• Zij werkt voor een firma die meubels verkoopt. (She works for a firm that sells furniture.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Weet je wat hij vanavond gaat doen? — Hij heeft een diner met een vriend die in Parijs woont. (Do you know what he is going to do tonight? — He has a dinner with a friend who lives in Paris.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, job interviews ("sollicitatiegesprekken") often focus on both qualifications and personality fit with the company culture. It's common to discuss not just your skills, but also how you collaborate and adapt to new environments.

sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dus" is a conjunction meaning "so" and is often used to link thoughts or conclusions.  
• "Dan" can mean "then" and is used to indicate a time or condition.  
• "Kunnen" is the modal verb "can" or "be able to," and it is placed in the second position of the clause.  
• "Nog" means "still" or "yet," indicating the continuation of a possibility.  
• "Afspreken" is an infinitive verb meaning "to meet" or "to arrange to meet." In Dutch, infinitive verbs are often placed at the end of the clause.

welke.spelling: The 'w' in Dutch is pronounced closer to an English 'v', while 'e' is short, creating /ɛ/.
welke.fast: The initial /ʋ/ in ‘welke’ may be pronounced as a [v] when followed by a vowel in fast speech.

dagen.spelling: The 'g' in 'dagen' is pronounced as /ɣ/ in the south and /x/ in the north of the Netherlands.
dagen.fast: The final /n/ in 'dagen' is often dropped in casual speech, resulting in 'dage'.

maandag.spelling: The vowel 'aa' represents the long /aː/ sound, typical in open syllables.
maandag.fast: The final /x/ in ‘maandag’ may be pronounced as a softer [χ] in casual speech.

tot.spelling: The word 'tot' follows the closed syllable pattern, resulting in a short vowel sound /ɔ/.
tot.fast: In connected speech, the final /t/ in 'tot' may become less aspirated or even assimilate with a following consonant.

vrijdag.fast: The final /x/ in ‘vrijdag’ may be softened or omitted in fast speech, especially in informal contexts.

maar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable.
maar.fast: In fast speech, the /r/ in 'maar ik' may be reduced or assimilated to the following vowel.

nederland.spelling: The open syllable 'nee-' indicates a long /eː/, while '-der-' and '-land' reflect standard Dutch vowel and consonant patterns.
nederland.fast: In rapid speech, the final /t/ in 'nederland' may be unreleased or slightly assimilated before a following consonant.

wel.spelling: The short vowel /ɛ/ is pronounced because the syllable is closed by the consonant /l/.
wel.fast: In connected speech, the /l/ in ‘wel ik’ might become a dark [ɫ] before a vowel.

hoe.spelling: The vowel sound /uː/ in 'hoe' is represented by the letters 'oe', a common Dutch spelling for this sound.
hoe.fast: In rapid speech, the /ˈɦuː/ in ‘hoe gaat’ may blend, with the /ɦ/ becoming less pronounced, sounding like /uːɣaːt/.

weet.spelling: Open syllable we- indicates a long /eː/ sound.
weet.fast: In rapid speech, final /t/ in ‘weet ik’ may become a glottal stop [ʔ] before a vowel.

rules.name: -eren
rules.how: Some het-words form their plural with -eren instead of -en.

rules.name: Sound shift
rules.how: The short vowel becomes long in the plural, because it ends up in an open syllable (da-gen).

rules.name: Latin plurals
rules.how: Latin nouns keep a Latin plural: -cus becomes -ci, and -um becomes -a.

rules.name: No plural
rules.how: Some nouns have no plural, such as uncountable substances. They take a singular verb, and 'veel' goes with the singular.
